name: Andrew Bobola
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Andrew Bobola was a Polish Jesuit priest whose ministry included preaching, catechesis and organizing lay groups to serve prisoners and children. After studying in Vilnius, he worked in several communities in a region where political conflict and religious divisions frequently overlapped.

During outbreaks of plague he and his collaborators cared for those affected. His later ministry brought him to Pinsk during war between regional powers. Captured by Cossacks in 1657, he refused to abandon his Catholic faith and was killed. The Jesuit account identifies him as a saint and martyr.

name: Francis Borgia
feast_note: October 3 is Francis Borgia’s Jesuit commemoration recorded by Nominis; September 30 is his Roman Martyrology date.
biography: Francis Borgia moved from a life of Spanish court service and family responsibilities into the Society of Jesus. He married Leonor de Castro, raised eight children and served as duke of Gandía. After his wife's death, he prepared to become a Jesuit while arranging his children's affairs.

He relinquished his title and was ordained a priest. Elected the Jesuits' third superior general in 1565, he oversaw schools, missions and the developing organization of the order. He died in Rome in 1572 after illness interrupted a journey. His biography illustrates a vocation that developed through several distinct stages of life.

name: Joseph Pignatelli
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Joseph Pignatelli was a Spanish-born Jesuit priest who helped his companions survive expulsion and the suppression of their order. Before exile, his work included teaching boys and visiting prisoners. When the Jesuits were expelled from Spain in 1767, he accompanied them instead of seeking an exemption through his noble family.

He maintained contact with dispersed former Jesuits and later joined a community connected with the surviving Society in Russia. He renewed his vows in 1797 and helped train new members. He died in 1811 before the order's worldwide restoration. The linked source disagrees internally about his death month; only the year is retained here.

name: Alphonsus Rodriguez
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Alphonsus Rodriguez was a Spanish Jesuit brother whose best-known work was welcoming people at the college of Montesión in Palma, Majorca. Before entering religious life, he managed a family business and married. The deaths of his wife and children, followed by business difficulties, preceded his renewed search for a religious vocation.

As the college's doorkeeper he received visitors, delivered messages and helped people seeking assistance. Students also approached him for advice and prayer. He became a friend and mentor to Peter Claver, encouraging his interest in overseas missions. His spiritual notes became known after his death in 1617.

name: Peter Faber
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Peter Faber belonged to the first companions of Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier in Paris. As a priest, he celebrated the Mass at Montmartre in 1534 during which the companions made their commitments. That group became the nucleus of the Society of Jesus.

When Ignatius left Paris in 1535, Faber cared for the companions and helped their community grow. He guided Claude le Jay, Jean Codure, and Paschase Broët through conversation and the Spiritual Exercises. His contribution to the emerging order included sustaining friendships as well as welcoming new members.

His later work took him through a Europe divided by religious conflict. The Society of Jesus's account describes his efforts toward understanding at Worms and Ratisbon, alongside teaching and preaching. His Memorial records an inner life of prayer that accompanied these journeys. He died in Rome in 1546, shortly after arriving exhausted from Coimbra.

In a 2014 homily, Pope Francis presented Faber's gentleness and ability to form friendships as central to his ministry. Francis connected Faber's prayer with his willingness to travel and speak with others, emphasizing love rather than condemnation in proclaiming the Gospel. This is a later spiritual interpretation of his example, distinct from a contemporary record of his travels.

Pope Francis: Homily at the Church of the Gesù, January 3, 2014

name: Edmund Arrowsmith
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Edmund Arrowsmith was born Brian Arrowsmith in Lancashire and took the name Edmund at confirmation while studying at the English College in Douai. After his ordination, he returned to Lancashire in 1613. He spent the following years ministering to Catholics under laws restricting their religious practice.

He joined the Jesuits in 1623 while continuing his pastoral work. An earlier imprisonment ended in release, but a later arrest led to conviction for being a priest. He was executed in 1628. Brian and Edmund refer to this same individual and are indexed here as alternate names rather than separate saints.

name: Henry Morse
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Henry Morse was an English convert who became a Catholic priest and Jesuit after studying abroad. His ministry was repeatedly interrupted by imprisonment and exile. While held at York Castle, he completed the spiritual retreat required for his Jesuit formation with the help of another imprisoned priest.

In London he cared for people during a plague outbreak, obtaining medicine and ministering to the dying. Later assignments took him back to northern England, where he was again captured. Brought to London for trial, he was condemned and executed in 1645. The Jesuit biography presents both his pastoral service and martyrdom.

name: Henry Walpole
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Henry Walpole was an English Jesuit priest whose vocation was influenced by Edmund Campion's martyrdom. He left legal studies for priestly formation, entered the Society of Jesus in 1584 and later served English Catholic soldiers abroad. He also worked at the English seminary in Valladolid.

He returned to England in 1593 but was arrested soon after landing in Yorkshire. Months of imprisonment and torture followed, including detention in the Tower of London. At his trial he refused the oath recognizing the monarch's religious supremacy. He was executed at York in 1595, after very little opportunity for ministry in his homeland.

name: John de Brito
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: John de Brito was a Portuguese Jesuit priest who worked in the Madura mission in India. Born into a family connected with the royal court, he entered the Jesuits as a teenager and travelled to Goa after ordination. His missionary work included adapting his clothing and manner of life to local ascetic customs.

After an earlier imprisonment he returned to Portugal to report on the mission, then chose to go back to India. His later arrest ended in execution at Oriyur. The institutional biography identifies him as a saint, but its detailed chronology contains inconsistencies; this summary retains the broad sequence and life years without asserting a disputed day.

name: Robert Southwell
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Robert Southwell was an English Jesuit priest and writer who served Catholics in and around London. Educated on the continent, he entered the Jesuits in Rome and was ordained in 1584. Two years later he returned to England, where Catholic ministry exposed priests and their hosts to arrest.

His work included visiting prisoners, assisting other priests and helping produce religious books through a secret press. Letters of encouragement became his work An Epistle of Comfort. After capture he endured torture and imprisonment while continuing to write poetry. He was executed in 1595 and is commemorated by the Jesuits as a saint and martyr.

name: Alexander Briant
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Alexander Briant was an English priest who studied at Oxford before crossing to the English College in Douai. After ordination in 1578, he returned to England and ministered in his home region. His period of pastoral work was cut short when men searching for another priest discovered him in a neighboring house.

His captors attempted to force information from him through deprivation and torture. He was eventually taken to the Tower of London. The Society of Jesus identifies him as a saint and records that he entered the Jesuits shortly before his execution in 1581. His brief life combined parish ministry with steadfastness during imprisonment.

name: David Lewis
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: David Lewis was a Welsh Jesuit priest remembered for decades of pastoral work in South Wales and particular care for people in poverty. After becoming Catholic, he studied in Rome, was ordained and entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1645. His return to Wales began a long period of local ministry.

That ministry was disrupted by the accusations surrounding Titus Oates's fabricated plot. Jesuits went into hiding as officials offered rewards for their capture. Lewis belongs to the Catholic martyrs of this persecution and died in 1679. The institutional account emphasizes his care for the poor as well as the dangers faced by Catholic clergy.

name: Philip Evans
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Philip Evans was a Welsh Jesuit priest who studied at Saint-Omer and returned to South Wales after ordination in 1675. He served Catholics there for four years, becoming known for charity and energetic pastoral work. His decision to remain became especially dangerous when anti-Catholic persecution intensified.

The false accusations associated with Titus Oates in 1678 were followed by rewards for the arrest of Jesuits. Evans was captured and imprisoned in Cardiff Castle. He was executed in 1679. His biography preserves a portrait of a priest who continued serving his community despite increasing pressure to leave the region.

name: Thomas Garnet
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Thomas Garnet was an English priest whose attempts to study and minister repeatedly brought imprisonment. Born in London, he attended the Jesuit college at Saint-Omer. A storm interrupted a journey to Spain and brought him into English custody, but he escaped and eventually completed his theological studies abroad.

Ordained in 1599, he returned to serve English Catholics. The example of his uncle Henry Garnet influenced his decision to enter the Jesuits in 1604. Religious persecution and the aftermath of the Gunpowder Plot disrupted his work. He died in 1608 and is identified as a saint by the Society of Jesus.

name: Anthony Daniel
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Anthony Daniel was a French Jesuit priest who became a missionary in New France after encounters with a Huron student and the missionary John de Brébeuf. Travelling with Brébeuf in 1634, he entered communities struggling with a devastating epidemic and suspicion directed toward the newcomers.

He taught children prayers and Christian teaching through music. A later attempt to run a boys' school in Quebec attracted few students and closed; Daniel returned to the missions. He worked for years at Cahiagué and died in 1648. Antoine Daniel is the French form of his name, not a separate missionary.

name: Charles Garnier
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Charles Garnier was a French Jesuit missionary who persisted in seeking an overseas assignment despite opposition from his family. In New France he first studied the Huron language and worked at Ossossané. He later travelled with Isaac Jogues to the Petun people, where their reception was initially difficult.

Epidemic disease and suspicion of the missionaries complicated those early visits. Garnier returned several times before establishing two missions during the winter of 1647. His biography traces this patient, interrupted work rather than an effortless expansion. He died in 1649 and is honored as a saint in the Society of Jesus.

name: Gabriel Lalemant
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Gabriel Lalemant was a French Jesuit priest who worked as a teacher and administrator before receiving permission to become a missionary. Poor health had complicated his repeated requests. He travelled to Quebec in 1646 and prepared for ministry by studying the language and customs of the people he would encounter.

In 1648 he went to Sainte-Marie, the mission headquarters in Huronia. His period of direct missionary work was short, and he became an assistant to John de Brébeuf shortly before their martyrdom. He died in 1649. His life connects educational service in France with the demanding preparation required for work in a different culture.

name: Noël Chabanel
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Noël Chabanel was a French Jesuit teacher who sought missionary work in New France but found the transition extremely difficult. Learning a new language and adapting to unfamiliar daily conditions challenged him. Although permitted to return to France, he chose to remain and made a commitment to persevere in the missions.

He worked with John de Brébeuf and later joined Charles Garnier at Etarita. When danger increased, he was sent back toward the mission headquarters. He died in 1649. The Jesuit account remembers a missionary whose continued service involved persistent struggle rather than easy adaptation or uninterrupted confidence.

name: René Goupil
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: René Goupil trained as a surgeon after poor health interrupted his first attempt to become a Jesuit. He nevertheless sought a way to serve the missions and went to New France as a lay helper. His medical skills offered a practical form of service to the missionary community.

In 1642 he accompanied Isaac Jogues on a journey from Quebec and was captured when their travelling party was attacked. He suffered in captivity and was killed that year. The Jesuit source records his reception into the Society shortly before death. Its geographical description is inconsistent, so this account does not assign an exact modern location to his journey.

feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: John de la Lande was a French layman who assisted the Jesuits in New France. Born in Dieppe, he worked with the community at Three Rivers before volunteering to accompany Isaac Jogues on a mission connected with peace negotiations. The journey brought them into a region troubled by warfare and distrust.

They continued despite warnings and were captured near the Mohawk village where Jogues had previously been held. De la Lande died in 1646. His birth date is not established in the institutional biography, and its death-date header needs further checking. His lay status is retained here; he is not described as a priest.

name: Francis Jerome
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Dates of death are not treated as feast days.
biography: Francis Jerome was an Italian Jesuit priest whose long ministry centered on Naples. Born near Taranto, he studied with the Theatines and Jesuits before entering the Society of Jesus in 1670. His early work included helping with retreats and missions in the diocese of Lecce.

After further theological preparation, he received the Naples mission as a permanent assignment and served there for about forty years. His collaborators included a sodality of artisans connected with the Gesù church. He died in 1716. Francesco de Geronimo and Francis Gerome are forms of the name used by the institutional source for this same saint.
